topic.original: Head of Instagram Adam Mosseri, wrote: “1.3 percent of people in the US spending 30-plus hours a week [on Instagram] sounds like a lot.” The staff member who conducted the research responded with a remark saying that it was a judgment call as to whether that was a big enough group to justify a response.
topic.final: Head of Instagram Adam Mosseri, wrote: “1.3 percent of people in the US spending 30-plus hours a week [on Instagram] sounds like a lot.” The staff member who conducted the research responded with a remark saying that it was a judgment call as to whether that was a big enough group to justify a response.

scope.core_proposition: Whether 1.3% of US Instagram users spending 30+ hours per week on the platform constitutes a population large and harmed enough to obligate Instagram's leadership to intervene with a product or policy response
on_scope_evidence: absolute headcount implied by the 1.3% figure versus the percentage framing
internal Meta/Instagram research on heavy and problematic use
validated problematic-use screening data (e.g., addiction-scale correlations with usage duration)
wellbeing outcomes correlated with 30+ hour weekly usage (sleep displacement, anxiety, depression)
revenue and engagement concentration among top-percentile users
precedent thresholds from gambling and alcohol industries on heavy-user dependence
public health prevalence thresholds used to trigger intervention (e.g., rare disease definitions, at-risk population sizing)
key_tensions: percentage framing (1.3% is small) versus absolute headcount framing (over a million people)
time-spent as a meaningful proxy for harm versus heavy use being benign or even valuable engagement
corporate duty-of-care thresholds: what prevalence level obligates a company to act against its own engagement metrics
user autonomy and anti-paternalism versus platform responsibility for compulsive-use patterns created by engagement-optimized design
off_scope_topics: general social media regulation and Section 230 debates
misinformation, content moderation, and election interference
data privacy and Cambridge Analytica-style scandals
Instagram's teen body-image research (a separate research thread from the same era)
Meta's other platforms (Facebook, WhatsApp) and metaverse strategy
drift_signatures: pivoting from the threshold question (when does a small percentage justify action) to broad anti-social-media or pro-regulation arguments
treating 30+ hours of weekly use as self-evidently harmful without evidence linking duration to wellbeing outcomes
citing extreme harms (self-harm, suicide, eating disorders) without tying them to the heavy-use cohort being debated
debating whether social media meets clinical addiction criteria instead of whether this usage level warrants a corporate response
shifting to government legislation when the topic is an internal company judgment call
scope.example_ceiling: Population-scale wellbeing harms (addiction-like use, sleep displacement, anxiety and depression) and corporate policy decisions; severe individual mental-health outcomes are proportionate only when linked to heavy-usage cohort data; existential or civilizational examples are disproportionate
scope.domain: social media platform governance, technology ethics, public health
excluded_scenarios: light or moderate users below the 30-plus-hours weekly threshold (implied)
explicit_qualifiers: 1.3 percent of people in the US
big enough group to justify a response

critique.rewritten_topic: Instagram's internal research found that 1.3% of US users spend 30+ hours a week on the app, yet leadership and the study's own researcher disagreed over whether that justified a response — one calling it 'a judgment call.' Under what conditions should a small minority of extremely heavy users push a platform to change its design, and through what mechanisms would that level of use actually harm them?

scope_additions.detail: Include teens and young users, parents, trust-and-safety researchers, executives, and regulators as parties with different stakes in where the response threshold sits.
Anchor to the 1.3% of US users at 30+ hours/week finding and the concrete decision of whether to build interventions such as time-limit prompts or usage caps.
Surface the engagement-revenue vs. user-wellbeing conflict and the meta-question of whether the 'judgment call' should rest with the company, independent researchers, or external oversight.

suggested_critique.rewritten_topic: Instagram's internal research found that 1.3% of US users spend 30+ hours a week on the app, yet leadership and the study's own researcher disagreed over whether that justified a response — one calling it 'a judgment call,' a split that may be less about the data than about who gets to define harm. Under what conditions should a small minority of extremely heavy users push a platform to change features like infinite scroll, through what mechanisms would that level of use actually harm them, and what evidence should settle that call?

scope_additions.detail: Name the design features under contention — infinite scroll, autoplay, push notifications, streaks — so claims about 'changing design' are testable rather than generic.

Capture the agency of heavy users themselves (including teens) plus parents and regulators: what heavy users want and intend, whether they experience their use as compulsive or chosen. Current BDI coverage is belief-heavy with thin Desires/Intentions modeling.

Treat the evidentiary threshold as itself contested: what would count as proof of harm (longitudinal mental-health outcomes, self-reported loss of control, displacement of sleep/school/work) versus leadership's 'judgment call' standard.
